prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In memory of my parents People whose lives have been shaped by history—and it is always tragic— do not want to talk about it, would rather dance, give parties on thrift-shop china. You feel wonderful in their homes, two leaky rooms, nests they stowed inside their hearts on the road into exile. They know how to fix potato peelings and apple cores so you smack your lips. The words start over again hold no terror for them. Obediently they rise and go with only a rucksack or tote bag. If they weep, it’s when you’re not looking. To tame their nightmares, they choose the most dazzling occupations, swallow the flames in the sunset sky, jump through burning hoops in their elegant tiger suits. Cover your eyes: there’s one walking on a thread thirty feet above us— shivering points of light leap across her body, and she works without a net.

Dedicated to the memory of my mother and father

Those whose existence has been molded by history—which is never anything but tragic—prefer silence over recounting it; they'd sooner dance and throw celebrations using dishes bought secondhand. Their houses make you feel marvelous, just a pair of drafty rooms, little shelters they carried tucked within their hearts along the path to banishment. They can transform potato skins and apple leftovers into something that leaves you licking your fingers. The phrase "begin again" doesn't frighten them. outputs.L3:
# Living in the Shadow of History

People whose lives have been shaped by tragic history often prefer to avoid discussing it. Rather than dwelling on the painful chapters of their past, they choose instead to celebrate and enjoy life, directing their energy toward the present rather than reliving what has already been endured.

This outlook is reflected in the homes they create. Even in the most humble surroundings, they cultivate a sense of warmth and comfort that makes their modest dwellings feel wonderful to visitors. Their ability to transform simple spaces into welcoming havens speaks to a deeper wisdom about what truly matters in life.

Having survived considerable hardship, they possess a remarkable resourcefulness. They know how to make the most of very little, stretching scarce resources and finding creative solutions where others might see only limitation. In their hands, even scraps can become satisfying meals—a testament to the ingenuity that adversity has taught them.

Their experiences with exile and displacement have left them with an unexpected gift: the loss of fear when facing new beginnings. Because they have already lost everything and rebuilt before, the idea of starting over holds no terror for them. They understand, in a way few others can, that life can be reconstructed from almost nothing.

Yet beneath this resilience lies a quieter truth. They keep their pain and grief carefully hidden, guarding their private sorrows away from public view. Behind their dazzling bravery and outward strength, they carry inner nightmares that they rarely reveal—masking their deepest wounds with a courage that both protects them and inspires those around them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem dedicated to parents who survived exile and historical trauma, focusing on their resilience, their refusal to speak of the past, and comparing them to circus performers.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Acrobats

You never told us how you crossed,
what borders bit into your feet,
what names you buried, what you lost—
you only taught us to repeat

the ordinary: *eat, be well,
the weather's cold, put on your coat.*
Behind each word, a locked hotel
of rooms you would not let us note.

I think of you as circus folk,
the ones who smile beneath the strain,
who lift the weight but never spoke
of how the muscle learned its pain.

You walked the wire above a past
that had no net, no second try,
and made the balance seem to last
as if you were not scared to die.

You caught each other, hand to wrist,
above the dark you would not name—
two people trained by what they missed
to trust the timing of the game.

And we, the children in the stands,
saw only how you did not fall,
the steady grace, the certain hands,
the act that made it look like all

was chosen, easy, meant to be.
We did not see the years of ache,
the practiced face, the guarantee
you made your bodies learn to fake.

You gave us silence like a gift,
a curtain drawn against the cold,
so we could sleep, so we could lift
our own small lives and not be told.

Now I applaud the empty air
where you once balanced, high and thin—
you who survived, who would not share,
who kept the whole performance in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse elegy in memory of refugee parents who chose joy over grief.
counterfactuals.output:
# What You Taught Me of Joy

You did not carry your losses
the way I expected—
no altar of ashes in the kitchen,
no shrine to the country that closed
its fist behind you.

Instead: the radio too loud on Sunday mornings,
your hips remembering a dance
from a village that no longer exists on any map,
the two of you laughing
at a joke told in a language
you were slowly forgetting.

I looked for grief in you
the way children look for proof
their parents are human—
and found it, yes,
but only in the small hours,
a shadow crossing your face
before you folded it away
like a letter you'd already read
a thousand times.

You chose the orange tree in the backyard.
You chose the neighbor's children
learning to say your names.
You chose to plant what you could not
bring across the water—
seeds in your coat pockets,
recipes in your hands,
songs that survived the crossing
because you kept singing them.

What did it cost you,
this joy?
I only understand now,
standing where you stood,
that it was never the absence of sorrow—
it was the harder thing:
sorrow, held, and set beside
a full table anyway.
Sorrow, and still the insistence
on butter, on music,
on being glad you were alive
to miss what you had lost.

You are gone now,
and I inherit not your wounds
but your stubborn brightness,
the way you turned toward the light
like something that had decided,
against all evidence,
to grow.

I set the radio too loud.
I dance in the kitchen.
I teach my children your names.

This is how I keep you—
not weeping,
but blooming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about immigrants who lived through tragic history but preferred dancing and celebration to talking about their suffering.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Ones Who Danced**

They came with suitcases of silence,
folded grief between the linens,
tucked old countries in their pockets—
the burning streets, the midnight knock,
the names they could no longer speak.

You'd ask them once, and only once,
about the years they crossed the water,
and they would wave a weathered hand
as if to brush away a fly,
then reach instead for the accordion.

*Come, come*, they'd say, *the soup is ready.*
*Come, come*, they'd say, *the music's playing.*
And in the kitchen small as memory
they'd spin the daughters, spin the sons,
their laughter louder than the past.

They knew what words could not resurrect.
They knew that mourning has its limits,
that a body built for burial
could also be a body built for joy—
so they chose joy, defiant, whole.

The wedding tables groaned with plenty.
The old songs rose in the old language.
Their feet remembered every step
of dances danced in vanished villages
by people who no longer breathed.

This was their monument, their prayer:
not stone, not speech, but movement—
the living proof that they survived,
that something tender crossed the ocean
and refused, refused, to die.

And when at last they too were gone,
we understood the thing they taught us:
that celebration is a language,
that every plate of shared abundance
was a sentence in their testimony.

They did not want our pity, only
this—that we would fill the room,
would pour the wine, would take a partner,
and dance the way they taught us how:
like people who have earned their gladness.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a moving poem that uses circus imagery—tightrope walkers, tiger suits, burning hoops—to describe survivors of displacement and their quiet strength.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Traveling Show

They taught us to smile beneath the paint,
to make the impossible look like grace—
each border a tightrope strung across the dark,
no net below, only the memory
of the ground we used to stand on.

*Watch how she crosses.*

My mother wears a tiger's suit,
the stripes she stitched from what they called her wildness,
her softness caged behind a beauty
sharp enough to frighten those who'd cage her.
She has learned to leap through burning hoops
and land as if the fire never touched her—

but I have seen her hands at night,
still trembling from the heat.

We are the ones who fold ourselves
into suitcases and songs,
who carry tents instead of houses,
who pitch our lives in fields
that were never meant to hold us,
then move again before the dawn.

*Applause. Applause.*

They love the spectacle of our endurance,
the way we balance everything we've lost
on the thin wire of a single day.
They do not see the practice—
the falling, and the falling,
and the getting up to fall again.

But listen:

there is a strength that does not roar.
It is the quiet of the acrobat
mid-air, suspended
between the country that released her
and the one that has not caught her yet—

that breath,
that held and holy breath,
where she becomes her own arriving.

We are still here.
We have crossed on nothing
but the rope of our own spines,
and we have not looked down.

*The lights go out. We bow. We stay.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled "In memory of my parents" about people shaped by tragic history who make you feel welcome in their modest home and hide their tears.
counterfactuals.output:
# In Memory of My Parents

They set the table with a careful grace,
each plate a small cathedral of their care,
and though I came a stranger to that place,
they made a room for me already there.

Their hands had learned what history can take—
the vanished names, the borders redrawn twice,
the houses left, the promises they'd break
who swore that they would keep them. Such a price

they paid in silence. Yet they poured the tea
and asked about my journey, asked my name,
and something in the way they looked at me
was welcome offered like a sheltered flame.

I saw it once—a brightness in the eye
my mother quickly turned toward the wall,
the small pretense, the reason to walk by
the window, so I would not see it fall.

They hid their tears the way they hid the years,
folded like linen in a drawer kept shut,
and taught me that the tenderest of fears
is love that will not let its grief be cut

into the open. This was how they gave:
not with the wound displayed, but with the bread,
the second helping, everything they'd save
so I would leave their table warm and fed.

Now they are gone, and I set out the plates.
I pour for strangers. When I feel it start—
that trembling at the door where sorrow waits—
I turn toward the window, like my heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
